input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a widely used separation technique, and in the case considered here it is being applied in order to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by contacting the stream with an organic solvent into which the acetic acid preferentially passes. One of the key quantities that characterises the system is the distribution coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase to its concentration in the aqueous phase when the two phases are in equilibrium with one another. For this system the distribution coefficient has a value of 0.53 at 25 °C, which means that at equilibrium the concentration in the aqueous phase is actually the higher of the two. The design that has been developed for this separation makes use of 7 countercurrent stages, and the predicted recovery that is obtained from the design calculation is 99% of the acetic acid present in the feed, which is a very high level of recovery. It is important to appreciate, however, that this prediction rests on certain assumptions that have been built into the calculation, most notably the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two liquid phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used, and so the predicted figure should be treated with an appropriate degree of caution. With a distribution coefficient of 0.53, the solvent does not take up the acid strongly in any single contact, and a recovery of 99% is an ambitious figure to reach on that basis; the predicted 99% depends entirely on the staging delivering what the equilibrium assumption promises at every step.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 0.53 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity fixes the character of the separation: at equilibrium the aqueous phase holds the higher concentration, and recovery has to be built from repeated contact rather than from a strong preference of the solute for the solvent. The design uses 7 countercurrent stages. Across the stage sequence the predicted recovery is 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. Countercurrent contact is what makes a high recovery compatible with a coefficient of 0.53, because the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous stream and the driving force is held up along the whole cascade. Recovery here is a fraction of the feed: it states how much of the acetic acid entering in the aqueous stream leaves in the organic stream, and the part not recovered leaves with the treated aqueous stream. A design can therefore be read at two levels, the coefficient fixing what one contact can do and the stage count fixing how far the sequence of contacts carries the separation. The prediction carries its assumptions with it. Every stage is treated as an equilibrium stage, and the mutual solubility of the two phases is treated as negligible. Under those two assumptions the stage calculation gives 99%. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A real stage that falls short of equilibrium, or a solvent pair with appreciable mutual solubility, moves the recovery away from the predicted value in a direction the calculation does not test. The 99% recovery is a model result for the stated coefficient, temperature, and stage count; performance of the extraction on the actual solvents is unmeasured.
